title: NES says it’s falling behind on its tree trimming efforts, advocates worry rushing could damage tree canopy

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Nashville Electric Services (NES) says it’s falling significantly behind on its tree trimming efforts months after moving to a more aggressive program after 2026’s ice storm.

During Wednesday’s NES board meeting, the utility company revealed it had only completed trimming on 89 miles across Nashville through August compared to the 2,258 miles it had hoped to complete by this point in the fiscal year.

NES says it did complete its previous four-year trimming cycle by June 30.

CEO Teresa Broyles-Aplin said the current shortfall comes as new contractors are still ramping up crews. She also said a vendor processing LiDAR data took longer than expected to get tree-trimming work plans to NES.

Wednesday, the board voted to allow Broyles-Aplin to move forward with additional vegetation-management contracts totaling up to $15 million without waiting for the October board meeting.

NES says the contracts will be awarded through its bidding process. The utility will report the selected vendors and contract amounts back to the board in October.

Earlier this year, the company moved from a 10 foot to 15 foot required clearance around power lines and sped up its trimming cycle from four years to three.

But many Nashvillians say they’ve been frustrated with the execution, saying NES crews have left their trees damaged and in danger of falling or dying.

“We get about an inquiry every week from residents who are asking about this and what we can do,” said Executive Director of the Nashville Tree Conservation Corps (NTCC) Stephanie Mahnke. “We had several folks who have heritage trees, really old trees that, of course, you know, are really difficult to replace that are being cut down entirely.”

NES says it uses professional crews and follow industry standards to protect the health of the trees.

NTCC has been meeting with representatives from NES and the city of Nashville to encourage them to be more diligent about protecting the tree canopy.

Mahnke says the conversations have been productive, but she worries that a push to catch up on trimming could lead to rushed work and more damage.

She says they hope to have more meetings with stakeholders to find a happy medium.

“There’s a way to do this alongside, to have the natural resources move alongside the evolution of the city,” she said. “I think the best we could have done so far was they agreed to more stakeholder meetings with advocacy groups like ours.”

She says she’s also hoping to make sure the new contractors that are brought in to help NES catch up are properly certified.

“We had brought this up in our meeting with NES last month, checking to see if their contractors are certified,” Mahnke said. “They were unsure about it. So that’s something that we’re looking at to see the new contractors are certified to do this.”
